subjective.topic: History, Classification and Acellular Organisms
subjective.question: Write a short note on the Golden Age of Microbiology.
subjective.answer: The Golden Age of Microbiology (about 1857-1914) was the period in which microbiology developed into a proper science. Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation, gave the germ theory of fermentation and developed pasteurization and vaccines. Robert Koch established pure-culture techniques and his postulates linking a specific microbe to a specific disease. Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery, and the causative agents of many major diseases were identified during this period.

subjective.topic: History, Classification and Acellular Organisms
subjective.question: On what basis are living organisms divided into three domains? Name the three domains.
subjective.answer: Organisms are divided into three domains on the basis of differences in their ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequences, as proposed by Carl Woese. The three domains are: (1) Bacteria - prokaryotes with peptidoglycan cell walls; (2) Archaea - prokaryotes that lack peptidoglycan and often live in extreme environments; and (3) Eukarya - all organisms with a true membrane-bound nucleus, including protists, fungi, plants and animals.

subjective.topic: History, Classification and Acellular Organisms
subjective.question: Why are viruses called acellular organisms?
subjective.answer: Viruses are called acellular because they are not made of cells. A virus particle (virion) consists only of a nucleic acid core, DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein coat (capsid) and sometimes an envelope. Viruses have no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no machinery for energy production or protein synthesis, so they cannot reproduce on their own. They multiply only inside living host cells, which is why they are called obligate intracellular parasites.

subjective.topic: Prokaryotic Cell: Characteristics, Wall and Membrane
subjective.question: Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
subjective.answer: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid, whereas eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum, which eukaryotes possess. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, while eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S. In most bacteria the DNA is not associated with histone proteins, whereas eukaryotic DNA is wound around histones. Most prokaryotes also possess a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, which is absent from eukaryotic animal cells.

subjective.topic: Prokaryotic Cell: Characteristics, Wall and Membrane
subjective.question: What is peptidoglycan? Write its composition and functions.
subjective.answer: Peptidoglycan is the rigid, mesh-like polymer that forms the main structural layer of the bacterial cell wall. It is composed of alternating sugar units, N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), joined in long chains and cross-linked by short peptide bridges. Its functions are to give the cell its shape, provide mechanical strength and rigidity, and protect the cell from bursting due to osmotic pressure (osmotic lysis). It is also the target of lysozyme and of antibiotics such as penicillin.

subjective.topic: Prokaryotic Cell: Characteristics, Wall and Membrane
subjective.question: Write the functions of the bacterial cell wall.
subjective.answer: The bacterial cell wall (1) maintains the characteristic shape of the cell, (2) provides rigidity and mechanical protection, (3) prevents the cell from bursting in a hypotonic environment by resisting osmotic pressure, (4) serves as an anchoring site for flagella and pili, and (5) contributes to the pathogenicity and staining behaviour of the bacterium, as in the Gram staining reaction.

subjective.topic: Prokaryotic Cell: Characteristics, Wall and Membrane
subjective.question: Differentiate between Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell walls.
subjective.answer: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer (many layers) and contain teichoic acids, but they have no outer membrane; they retain the crystal violet stain and appear purple. Gram-negative bacteria have a very thin peptidoglycan layer but possess an additional outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) outside the peptidoglycan; they lose the crystal violet on decolourization and appear pink after counterstaining with safranin.

subjective.topic: Prokaryotic Cell: Characteristics, Wall and Membrane
subjective.question: Write the functions of the cell (cytoplasmic) membrane.
subjective.answer: The cytoplasmic membrane (1) acts as a selectively permeable barrier that controls the entry of nutrients and the exit of waste products, (2) is the site of energy generation, because the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis are located in it, (3) carries enzymes for respiration, photosynthesis (in photosynthetic bacteria) and synthesis of cell wall and capsule components, (4) helps in the secretion of enzymes and toxins, and (5) anchors DNA during cell division through its invaginations.

subjective.topic: Prokaryotic Cell: Characteristics, Wall and Membrane
subjective.question: What is the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane?
subjective.answer: The fluid mosaic model, proposed by Singer and Nicolson, describes the cell membrane as a phospholipid bilayer in which protein molecules are embedded like a mosaic. The phospholipid molecules can move laterally, giving the membrane a fluid character, while the proteins float in the bilayer and perform functions such as transport, enzymatic activity and reception of signals. Carbohydrates attached to proteins and lipids on the outer surface form the glycocalyx in eukaryotic cells.

subjective.topic: Flagella and Pili
subjective.question: Write the parts of a bacterial flagellum.
subjective.answer: A bacterial flagellum consists of three parts: (1) the filament - the long, hollow, helical part made of the protein flagellin, which extends outwards from the cell surface; (2) the hook - a short, curved, flexible part that connects the filament to the basal body; and (3) the basal body - a rod with a series of rings that anchors the flagellum in the cell wall and membrane and works as a motor that rotates the filament.

subjective.topic: Flagella and Pili
subjective.question: Write the different arrangements of flagella on bacterial cells.
subjective.answer: On the basis of the number and arrangement of flagella, bacteria are classified as: (1) monotrichous - a single flagellum at one pole, e.g. Vibrio cholerae; (2) amphitrichous - a single flagellum at each of the two poles; (3) lophotrichous - a tuft of flagella at one or both poles, e.g. Spirillum; (4) peritrichous - flagella distributed all over the cell surface, e.g. Escherichia coli; and (5) atrichous - bacteria without flagella.

subjective.topic: Flagella and Pili
subjective.question: Define the term pili and write its functions.
subjective.answer: Pili are short, thin, hair-like protein appendages present on the surface of many bacteria; they are shorter and thinner than flagella and are made of the protein pilin. Their functions are: (1) attachment - pili and fimbriae help the bacterium adhere to surfaces, tissues and host cells, which is important in causing infection; and (2) conjugation - a special long sex pilus forms a bridge between a donor and a recipient bacterium through which plasmid DNA is transferred from one cell to the other.

subjective.topic: Flagella and Pili
subjective.question: Differentiate between pili and flagella.
subjective.answer: Flagella are long, thick, helical appendages made of flagellin whose function is cell motility (swimming). Pili are much shorter, thinner and more numerous appendages made of pilin; they are not used for movement but for attachment to surfaces and, in the case of the sex pilus, for conjugation. Flagella arise from a basal body and rotate like a propeller, whereas pili simply project from the cell surface.

subjective.topic: Culture Media and Agar
subjective.question: What is agar? Why is it used as a solidifying agent in culture media?
subjective.answer: Agar is a polysaccharide obtained from red algae (seaweed such as Gelidium). It is used as a solidifying agent because it melts at about 100 degrees C but does not solidify until about 40 degrees C, so heat-sensitive nutrients and even bacterial cells can be mixed with it without damage. Once solid, it remains firm at incubation temperatures, and because very few microorganisms can digest agar, the medium stays solid during growth. It is also transparent and inert, so it does not interfere with the growth of bacteria.

subjective.topic: Culture Media and Agar
subjective.question: Enlist the classes of media based on their function.
subjective.answer: On the basis of function, culture media are classified as: (1) enriched media - contain extra nutrients such as blood or serum for fastidious organisms, e.g. blood agar; (2) enrichment media - liquid media that favour the growth of a desired organism while suppressing others; (3) selective media - contain inhibitors that allow only certain organisms to grow, e.g. MacConkey agar; (4) differential media - distinguish between organisms by colony appearance, e.g. MacConkey agar differentiating lactose fermenters; (5) transport media - preserve specimens during transport; and (6) anaerobic and assay media used for special purposes.

subjective.topic: Culture Media and Agar
subjective.question: Differentiate between selective and differential media, giving one example of each.
subjective.answer: Selective media contain substances that inhibit the growth of unwanted organisms and allow only the desired organisms to grow; for example, MacConkey agar contains bile salts and crystal violet that inhibit Gram-positive bacteria and select Gram-negative enteric bacteria. Differential media do not necessarily inhibit growth but distinguish between organisms by a visible change in the medium or colonies; for example, on MacConkey agar lactose-fermenting colonies appear pink while non-lactose fermenters remain colourless.

subjective.topic: Sterilization and Chemical Control of Microorganisms
subjective.question: What are the conditions and uses of a hot air oven?
subjective.answer: A hot air oven sterilizes by dry heat, and the standard condition is 160 degrees C maintained for 2 hours (alternatively 170 degrees C for 1 hour). Dry heat kills microorganisms by oxidation of their cell components. The hot air oven is used for articles that are damaged by moisture or steam, such as glassware (Petri dishes, pipettes, flasks), metal instruments, oils, greases and dry powders. It is not suitable for culture media, rubber items or heat-sensitive materials.

subjective.topic: Sterilization and Chemical Control of Microorganisms
subjective.question: What is dry heat sterilization? Give its methods and applications.
subjective.answer: Dry heat sterilization is the killing of microorganisms by hot, dry air or direct flame, acting mainly through oxidation. Its methods include flaming (sterilizing inoculating loops and needles in a flame), incineration (burning of contaminated waste), and the hot air oven (160 degrees C for 2 hours). It is used for glassware, metal instruments, oils and powders that cannot be sterilized by moist heat, because moisture does not penetrate them properly or would damage them.

subjective.topic: Sterilization and Chemical Control of Microorganisms
subjective.question: Enlist the characteristics of an ideal antibacterial chemical.
subjective.answer: An ideal antibacterial (antimicrobial) chemical should: (1) kill or inhibit pathogens effectively, preferably over a broad spectrum; (2) not damage the tissues of the host or the material being disinfected; (3) act rapidly and remain active in the presence of organic matter; (4) be stable during storage and soluble in water or alcohol; (5) be non-corrosive and non-staining; (6) have good penetrating power; and (7) be inexpensive and easy to use.

subjective.topic: Sterilization and Chemical Control of Microorganisms
subjective.question: Name three chemical compounds that disrupt the cell membrane of bacteria.
subjective.answer: Three groups of chemicals that kill bacteria by disrupting (damaging) their cell membrane are: (1) phenol and phenolics, such as cresols, which denature proteins and disrupt the membrane; (2) alcohols, such as 70 percent ethanol and isopropanol, which dissolve membrane lipids and denature proteins; and (3) detergents, especially cationic detergents such as quaternary ammonium compounds (benzalkonium chloride), and bisbiguanides such as chlorhexidine, which alter membrane permeability and cause leakage of cell contents.

subjective.topic: Sterilization and Chemical Control of Microorganisms
subjective.question: What are the factors that influence the bacterial death rate?
subjective.answer: The rate at which bacteria are killed by a physical or chemical agent depends on: (1) the number of microorganisms present - a larger population takes longer to kill; (2) the nature of the population - endospores and older or more resistant species die more slowly; (3) the concentration or intensity of the agent; (4) the duration of exposure; (5) the temperature at which the agent acts; (6) the presence of organic matter such as blood, pus or faeces, which reduces the effectiveness of disinfectants; and (7) local conditions such as pH and moisture. Death occurs at a constant (logarithmic) rate, so a fixed proportion of the surviving cells dies in each successive unit of time.

subjective.topic: Biochemical Tests and Microbial Disease
subjective.question: What is the catalase test? Explain it step by step.
subjective.answer: The catalase test detects the enzyme catalase, which decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, and is used to differentiate catalase-positive staphylococci from catalase-negative streptococci. Steps: (1) Place a small amount of the bacterial colony on a clean glass slide using a sterile loop or wooden applicator (avoid taking blood agar, which can give a false positive). (2) Add one drop of 3 percent hydrogen peroxide over the colony. (3) Observe immediately. (4) Rapid bubbling or effervescence due to the release of oxygen indicates a positive test; no bubbling indicates a negative test.

subjective.topic: Sterilization and Chemical Control of Microorganisms
subjective.question: Differentiate between sterilization and disinfection.
subjective.answer: Sterilization is the complete removal or destruction of all forms of microbial life, including bacterial endospores, from an object; it is achieved by methods such as autoclaving and hot air oven. Disinfection is the destruction of vegetative pathogens (but not necessarily endospores) on inanimate objects by chemical agents called disinfectants, while the same process on living tissues is called antisepsis and the chemicals used are antiseptics.

subjective.topic: Biochemical Tests and Microbial Disease
subjective.question: What is rat bite fever? Name its causative agents.
subjective.answer: Rat bite fever is a bacterial disease of humans acquired through the bite or scratch of an infected rat (or through food or water contaminated with rat urine, called Haverhill fever). It is characterized by relapsing fever, chills, muscle pain, rash and joint pain at intervals after the bite wound appears to heal. It is caused by two bacteria: Streptobacillus moniliformis, the common cause in most regions, and Spirillum minus, which causes the form known as sodoku, common in Asia.
